item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers Get Boost in Tarik Skubal Free Agency Pursuit
item.dc:creator: Aaron Coloma
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers free agent starting pitcher Tarik Skubal is the best free agent on the market this offseason, with some experts believing he could receive a deal in excess of $400 million. According to ESPN's Alden Gonzalez, though, the two-time Cy Young-winning left-hander may command a lower price than that, which is good news for the Dodgers, who will definitely be in the race to maintain him. item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers free agent starting pitcher Tarik Skubal is the best free agent on the market this offseason, with some experts believing he could receive a deal in excess of $400 million.
According to ESPN's Alden Gonzalez, though, the two-time Cy Young-winning left-hander may command a lower price than that, which is good news for the Dodgers, who will definitely be in the race to maintain him.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto currently holds the largest pitcher contract by total value in MLB history at $325 million, which may have been possible for Skubal a couple of years ago, but Gonzalez believes Skubal is being held back by a few factors.
"But he's also 30 years old, at a time when pitchers break down and teams are only willing to dole out massive contracts to players at earlier ages, with a recent elbow surgery to boot," Gonzalez wrote. "Skubal clearly won't get the 12-year deal that allowed Yamamoto's guarantee to stretch so high, and some executives have a hard time believing he'll get 10. Said one: 'The price will be huge, but I don't think he's touching 400.'"
Why is This Good News for the Dodgers?
The Dodgers aren't any strangers to handing out big, long contracts, but Katie Woo of The Athletic doesn't see them doing the same with a 10-year, $400 million deal with Skubal.
'I can't see [Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman] stomaching a 10-year, $400 million contract if it gets up that high," Woo said on 97.1 The Fan.
"The only way I see the Dodgers really being fierce competitors for Skubal is if Skubal is willing to take a deal similar to the structure and the concept like Kyle Tucker.
"Obviously, the money and the monetary values are going to be different, but if you can get a shorter-term, three-to-four-year contract with opt-outs and a super high AAV, that's, I think, the only way that we can see the Dodgers being real major players for Skubal."
The Dodgers signed Tucker to a four-year, $240 million deal last offseason, and his $60 million annual average value is second on the team only to Shohei Ohtani. The Dodgers are more than capable of handing out a deal of that size, and could very well do so if they see Skubal in their long-term plans.
Does Tarik Skubal Deserve a Big Deal?
Skubal, 30, is without a doubt one of MLB's best pitchers, but entering the latter half of his MLB career, it's understandable that teams would offer him less than they would have a few years ago.
The southpaw will enter his eighth MLB season next year, fresh off of an elbow surgery in 2026 to remove loose bodies from his elbow. He had a 2.72 ERA across 26 starts with the Dodgers and the Detroit Tigers, striking out 186 batters in 158.2 innings pitched.
Those numbers aren't quite at the same level as his unbelievable 2024 and 2025 seasons, but they're also nothing to scoff at.
The better part of Skubal's season came with the Dodgers, as he had a 2.61 ERA through 10 starts to close the year, striking out 70 batters in 62 innings. He also had a good postseason, allowing just three runs through 11 innings for a 2.45 ERA.
Skubal's performances with the Dodgers proved he can be a functioning piece in the Dodgers' puzzle, and bringing him back on a deal similar to Tucker's would make a statement to the rest of the league following a disappointing end to the 2026 season.

item.content:encoded:
Christian Yelich Dedicates Brewers’ First World Series Title To Bob Uecker
Christian Yelich has waited a long time to call himself a World Series champion.
In the middle of the celebration, his thoughts turned to the man who wanted it as badly as anyone.
After the Milwaukee Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 to clinch the first championship in franchise history, Yelich spoke with FOX Sports’ Ken Rosenthal. Rosenthal asked what longtime Brewers broadcaster Bob Uecker would be thinking if he were looking down.
"He’s smiling, man. He’s smiling," Yelich said. "I really wish he could have been here to see this. … But like we said a bunch, he’s been with us a lot. We keep him close to our hearts. And this one’s still for Bob."
Bob Uecker, who died in 2025, was the longtime voice of the Brewers. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images)
Uecker, the voice of the Brewers for 54 seasons, died in January 2025 at 90 from small-cell lung cancer, months after calling his final Brewers postseason game. His diagnosis was never made public, but those closest to him knew, including Yelich.
During the Stand Up To Cancer moment in Game 4, every Brewers player’s placard read "UECK." (Photo by Mary DeCicco/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
Uecker’s memory followed the Brewers throughout October.
During Game 4 on Tuesday, play paused after the fifth inning for the annual Stand Up To Cancer moment, when everyone in the ballpark holds up a placard with the name of someone affected by cancer.
As cameras panned across the Brewers lined up in front of their dugout, every placard carried the same name: "UECK."
"It just feels like it’s fitting, the obvious choice to make," Yelich said afterwards.
Yelich has seen this Brewers run take shape since the day he arrived in Milwaukee.
Acquired from the Miami Marlins in January 2018, he won NL MVP in his first season in Milwaukee.
He’s now the second-longest-tenured Brewer behind Brandon Woodruff, and they’re the last two players left from the 2018 team that lost Game 7 of the NLCS to the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Eight years later, Milwaukee finally finished the job. The Brewers swept the Dodgers in the NLCS and then beat the Rays to bring home the city’s first World Series title.
"We’re coming home, baby," Yelich told Rosenthal when asked for his message to Brewers fans. "We can’t wait to see you. Can’t wait to celebrate."

item.title: [PCMag] Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays Livestream: How to Watch The MLB World Series Game 5 for Free
item.dc:creator: Jason Cohen

item.content:encoded:
The MLB World Series is finally here after several weeks of intense playoff action. The Brewers swept the Dodgers to reach the World Series for the first time in 44 years. The Rays beat out the Guardians in six games to win the American League pennant for just the third time. Just like in this year's WNBA Finals, we're about to witness history: Whoever wins, this will be the franchise's first championship.
The Milwaukee Brewers are currently in the lead with three wins; they only need one more to win the entire World Series. But it's still anyone's game. Which team will come out on top? Here's how you can watch tonight's World Series game live, even for free.
What Time Is the Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays Game?
Game 5 of the World Series between the Rays and Brewers will take place on Wednesday, October 28, at 8:00 p.m. ET.
How to Watch the Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays?
This year, the World Series will be broadcast on Fox and the Fox One app. You can also watch it with a live TV or sports streaming subscription from DirecTV, Fubo, Hulu, Sling, Sportsnet+ (if you're in Canada), or YouTube TV.
How to Watch the Brewers vs. Rays for Free
If you don't want to subscribe to any of the above platforms, you may be able to sign up for a few free trials to gain access to the remaining games. Fox One and Hulu offer three-day trials, DirecTV and Fubo offer five days, and YouTube TV gives you 10 days for free.
2026 MLB World Series Game Schedule
MLB's expanded postseason means more teams on the playoff schedule. In the Wild Card round, the Braves beat the Phillies, the Padres beat the Cubs, the Yankees defeated the Red Sox, and the White Sox defeated the Astros. The winners advanced to the Division Series, where the Los Angeles Dodgers, Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays, and Cleveland Guardians beat their respective opponents.
For the Championship Series, the Brewers beat the Dodgers in four games to clinch the National League pennant. The Rays defeated the Guardians in six games to capture the American League pennant. Now, Milwaukee and Tampa Bay will face off in the best-of-seven World Series to begin on October 23. Who will get to raise the trophy?
World Series: Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays - MIL leads 3-1
- Game 5 on October 28 - Fox/Fox One*
- Game 6 on October 30 - Fox/Fox One*
- Game 7 on October 31 - Fox/Fox One*
*if necessary
How to Stream the 2026 MLB Playoffs
This year's MLB postseason is stretched across multiple networks and streaming services. All Wild Card Series games for the American League and National League were broadcast on NBC, NBCSN, and Peacock. ALDS and ALCS games were on TBS/TruTV and HBO Max, while NLDS and NLCS games were on Fox/FS1. For the World Series, all games will be broadcast on Fox and the Fox One streaming service.
- DirecTV: DirecTV's MySports base pack costs $45 per month for the first six months to see every game on Fox, FS1, NBC, and TBS/TruTV.
- Fox One: Fox's own streaming app lets you watch the NLDS, NLCS, and World Series on Fox and FS1 for $20 per month.
- Fubo: Fubo's Sports plan costs $45.99 for the first month to watch the Wild Card Series, NLDS, NLCS, and World Series on Fox, FS1, and NBC/NBCSN.
- HBO Max: If you pay for the $18.49-per-month HBO Max Standard, you'll be able to watch the ALDS and ALCS games on TBS/TruTV.
- Hulu: For $90 per month, you can watch every game on Fox, FS1, NBC, TBS, and TruTV.
- Peacock: Instead of a live TV service, you'd need to pay $10.99 per month for Peacock Premium to see the Wild Card Series games.
- Sling: The $60.99-per-month Sling Orange & Blue bundle will let you watch the ALDS and ALCS on TBS/TruTV and the NLDS and NLCS on FS1. Day Passes are also available for Sling Orange, allowing you to watch games on TBS for up to seven days.
- Sportsnet+ (Canada only): The $30-per-month Standard tier lets you watch every postseason game.
- YouTube TV: Though the standard plan for YouTube TV costs $83 per month, you can actually now pay for the cheaper $65 Sports package to see all games on Fox, FS1, NBC/NBCSN, and TBS/TruTV.
Can I Watch Postseason Games on MLB.TV?
Are you already an MLB.TV subscriber? You can watch the Division Series, Championship Series, and World Series games through MLB's own streaming service—but there's a catch. To watch on MLB.TV, you'll first need to authenticate through a participating pay TV provider. It's such a sticking point that it makes the entire question moot. If you already have a TV provider, then you wouldn't need to use a streaming service. If you don't already have an MLB.TV subscription, don't pay for one now.
How can I listen to the 2026 postseason?
You can also listen to the games via ESPN Radio.
Which Teams Are In the Playoffs?
Since MLB expanded its postseason picture in 2022, a total of 12 teams make the playoffs each year. That includes six teams per league, including the three division winners and three Wild Card teams.
- American League Division Winners: Tampa Bay Rays (1), Cleveland Guardians (2), Houston Astros (3)
- American League Wild Card: New York Yankees (4), Boston Red Sox (5), Chicago White Sox (6)
- National League Division Winners: Milwaukee Brewers (1), Los Angeles Dodgers (2), Atlanta Braves (3)
- National League Wild Card: Chicago Cubs (4), Philadelphia Phillies (5), San Diego Padres (6)
Upgrade Your Streaming Experience
If you decide to watch the MLB postseason, there's still time to get a big-screen television for viewing this beautiful game. Pro tip: Turn on your TV's motion-smoothing option for the best picture while watching sports. Just remember to turn it off before watching other TV shows and movies to avoid the awful "soap opera" effect.
About Our Expert
As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert.
I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week.
My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth.
My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work.
Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays are favored to take Game 3 on Monday, but their chances of capturing their first ever World Series title have dwindled.
The Rays jumped out to a 4-0 first inning lead in Game 2, but through the game’s final eight innings the offense sputtered and the defense, nor pitching from ace Drew Rasmussen, was as sharp as needed to hold down the Brewers, who earned a 5-4 victory.
The pair of one-run victories in Milwaukee have put the Brewers in prime position for their first title. Nearly 81% of MLB teams that have generated a 2-0 series lead in the World Series have gone on to win the title.
To disrupt that statistic, the Rays will need to find a way to win Game 3. Kalshi traders make their odds 53% as of Monday morning.
For informational purposes only. Not trading advice. See full disclaimer below. Kalshi is the Official Prediction Market Partner of the Atlanta Braves, Los Angeles Dodgers, San Francisco Giants, San Diego Padres, and Boston Red Sox.
World Series Game 3 Odds: Rays favored in home ballpark
Right-handed pitcher Freddy Peralta had a rough start to his 2026 campaign when pitching for the New York Mets. But after being dealt to the Rays, he’s unlocked a former version of himself, one the Milwaukee Brewers know quite well. Peralta pitched for the Brewers for eight seasons before being traded to the Mets in the offseason. The Mets dealt him to the Rays at the trade deadline.
As such, now he’ll need to square off against his former team in World Series Game 3, looking to extend an incredible stretch of pitching which saw him earn ALCS MVP honors.
Across three starts and one relief appearance this postseason, Peralta has thrown 16.2 innings and allowed just two earned runs, good for a 1.08 ERA.
But the Brewers represent a level up offensively. Milwaukee finished the regular season tied for first in wRC+ against right-handed starters and led the league in on-base percentage and batting average against the handedness.
On the other hand, the Rays will draw left-handed starter Robert Gasser. Like the rest of the Milwaukee staff, Gasser has been fantastic this postseason, throwing nine innings over the course of two starts and allowing just one earned run.
Southpaws have been a challenge for the Rays this season, with the team ranking 26th against lefties in terms of wRC+ during the regular season. Even if they are able to get through Gasser, the Milwaukee bullpen features lefties JoJo Romero, DL Hall, and Aaron Ashby, and has been nearly unhittable, collectively posting a 1.23 ERA in nearly 51 innings this postseason.
Nevertheless, Kalshi traders make the Rays, who posted a 55-26 record at home during the regular season, slight favorites at 53% in Game 3.
The Rays overcame a 2-1 deficit in the ALCS, but they face a stiffer test against baseball’s top team in the World Series.
Regardless of the Game 3 winner, Game 4 will take place on Tuesday in Tampa Bay. In early trading, Kalshi traders make the Brewers slight favorites on the road in that game, pricing them at 50%.
Should a Game 5 be necessary, it will take place on Wednesday in Tampa Bay. If Games 6 or 7 are required, those will take place back in Milwaukee after a travel day.
Through two games, Brewers catcher William Contreras is the favorite for World Series MVP, according to Kalshi traders.
Contreras is trading around 38% to earn the award while outfielder Jackson Chourio is trading at 17% and left-handed reliever Aaron Ashby is priced at 15%.
In their two home victories, Contreras has notched four hits in eight at-bats and driven in two runs for Milwaukee. Plus, he’s thrown out multiple runners attempting to steal and helped manage a pitching staff through two tense one-run victories.
Chourio has posted similar stats, netting four hits in his nine at-bats, while stealing two bases and cutting down a runner at the plate with an outfield assist during Game 2.
Though less heralded coming into the series, Brewers reliever Aaron Ashby has been dominant all postseason, pitching 15.2 innings without allowing a single run. That includes more than three innings of World Series play in which he’s only allowed one hit.
Down 2-0, the highest priced Ray player is Junior Caminero, who is trading around 6% to win the award.

item.description: Tarik Skubal is going to be the top starting pitcher available in free agency this winter. He has won back-to-back American League Cy Young awards and will be highly sought after, which should make for a very interesting several weeks leading up to the likely implementation of a lockout. item.content:encoded:
Tarik Skubal is going to be the top starting pitcher available in free agency this winter. He has won back-to-back American League Cy Young awards and will be highly sought after, which should make for a very interesting several weeks leading up to the likely implementation of a lockout.
The Los Angeles Dodgers should be in the mix to retain his services for 2027 and beyond, but they are going to have competition from other big market teams. MLB.com’s Mark Feinsand listed several teams that could be in the mix for him, including the New York Mets.
Erik Beaston of Bleacher Report predicts that the Mets will ultimately be the ones to win the sweepstakes.
“If Los Angeles can do enough to prove to Skubal that this year was an anomaly and that the team is not the aging unit it looked like at times in the playoffs, one would have to figure they would be the front runner,” Beaston writes.
“The Mets, though, are a young team with pieces in Carson Benge, AJ Ewing, and Nolan McLean that have them set up nicely for the future. Add in future Hall of Famers Juan Soto and Francisco Lindor and you have a team that, with the right coaching, is a World Series contender.
“Even more so with Skubal in the rotation.”
New York Mets Predicted to Win Tarik Skubal Sweepstakes
Beaston goes on to say that the Dodgers window may be closing, while the Mets window may be opening. Despite having a down season, New York still does have a lot of solid young pieces in place, which sets them up well for the future.
With Skubal in the rotation, New York could have a good chance to bounce back into postseason contention after a rough 2026 season. They will have other areas of the roster that need to be focused on as well, but signing Skubal would be a good first step. They’re going to have to start somewhere, so adding the best starting pitcher in all of Major League Baseball might at least get them back on the map for contention.
Skubal made 26 starts in 2026, going 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA and striking out 186 batters over 158 2/3 innings of work during the regular season and pitched well for the Dodgers in the playoffs, so if the Mets do sign him, they’ll know exactly what they’re going to get, which is a very consistent top of the rotation starting pitcher.
The Downside of Signing Tarik Skubal
One thing the Mets would have to worry about is his injury history. He missed several starts earlier this year with the Detroit Tigers after undergoing surgery to remove bone chips in his elbow.
He made it back very quickly, but he has historically been a pitcher who has dealt with a lot of arm troubles, and that could be a potential downside of having to commit a high amount of money to him for a long-term contract.
He would make them a better team, but the Mets have had plenty of contracts go south for them in recent years.

item.content:encoded:
Padres get bold Tarik Skubal prediction that makes perfect sense originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The San Diego Padres are heading into the 2026-2027 MLB offseason with plenty of questions they'll need to answer. Mason Miller is locked in, but Adrian Morejon, their No. 2 reliever, is a free agent.
But they might have bigger fish to fry with their starting rotation. Michael King is likely to opt out and hit free agency, while multiple others are also set to hit the open market. So, adding a starter this Winter would make a lot of sense.
Will that starter be Tarik Skubal? Bleacher Report's Kerry Miller predicted the Padres would be the winners of the Skubal sweepstakes in a "bold prediction." But considering their need and the fit, this would actually make perfect sense for the team and player.
Padres predicted to sign Tarik Skubal in deal that makes perfect sense
"NL West: San Diego Padres win Tarik Skubal sweepstakes," Miller predicts. This prediction is considered "bold," but it might actually be one of Skubal's most sensible landing spots.
While there's been a ton of links between Skubal and the New York Mets, Los Angeles Dodgers, or even a return to the Detroit Tigers, the Padres should be considered a real landing spot for the left-handed Cy Young winner.
Skubal is going to seek top dollar this offseason, and with a new ownership group in charge, what better way to introduce themselves to the Padres' faithful than by being willing to spend a fortune on Skubal?
That's the kind of move that could endear a fanbase to its ownership group, something not often seen in professional sports.
But add in that A.J. Preller is more than willing to make a surprising move, and the major need in the rotation, and Skubal actually makes perfect sense for the Padres.
It might cost a fortune, likely upwards of $300 million over an extended period of time, but if the Padres want to invest in this team, with the belief they are serious World Series contenders these next few years, a Skubal signing is a very sensible decision.

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE – Jacob Misiorowski stepped on the mound for a World Series debut like no other.
“I had so much adrenaline built up,” he said.
Recommended Videos
He threw a pitch the likes of which had never been seen in the Fall Classic.
The Miz broke the World Series velocity record with his very first delivery, a 103.5 mph fastball to the Tampa Bay Rays’ Yandy Díaz that was taken high out of the strike zone for a ball. He allowed one run over five innings to get his first postseason win as a starter, helping the Milwaukee Brewers to a 3-2 victory in Friday night’s opener.
“I don’t even know how to tell you how I felt,” the 24-year-old right-hander said a half-hour after the end of a crazy ninth inning, prolonged by a game-extending video review. “I still don’t know how I felt. I feel like I’m still trying to take everything in and understand what happened.”
Misiorowski gave up four hits and one walk, striking out a season-low three.
Aroldis Chapman of the Chicago Cubs had the previous mark for fastest Series pitch at 103.2 mph in the ninth inning of Game 2 in 2016, an offering that resulted in a groundout to second by Cleveland’s Coco Crisp. The previous high by a Series starting pitcher since tracking began in 2008 was 101.1 mph by the New York Mets’ Noah Syndergaard to Kansas City’s Ben Zobrist that was taken for a ball in the first inning of Game 3 in 2015.
Miz reached 100 mph with 38 pitches, topping the previous Series high of 24 by Chapman in Game 5 of 2016. The most by a starting pitcher in the Series had been six by Tampa Bay’s Tyler Glasnow in the 2020 opener against the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Tampa Bay scored in the fourth when Jonathan Aranda walked, took third on Junior Caminero’s double over center fielder Garrett Mitchell and came around on Liam Hicks’ grounder to first baseman Jake Bauers.
Nearing the end of his first full major league season, Misiorowski has reached 100 mph with 134 of 260 postseason pitches. But his spin rate was down, a sign of a season in which he has pitched 188 innings — up from 141 1/3 innings last year. And he got just seven swings and misses, five on his fastball.
Tampa Bay batters fouled off 20 of his 78 pitches and tipped another.
During the regular season, Misiorowski reached 100 mph with 1,115 pitches, including a high of 105.5 mph to the Chicago Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 27.
“What we’re used to seeing in the regular season was Miz just mow through people and have two strikeouts an inning. That’s unrealistic,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said. “This is the best team in the American League.”
Miz's first pitch was so fast the scoreboard at American Family Field couldn't keep up, flashing 103.4 mph — one-tenth of a mile less than it registered on MLB’s Statcast system.
“He’s such a special pitcher,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “I felt like for him to be out of the game at five innings, there’s a small win in that.”
Misiorowski threw fastballs on 10 of his first 12 pitches, then mixed in more offspeed stuff. In all he tossed 48 fastballs, 17 cutters, seven sliders and six curveballs.
Miz finished with 30 pitches at 101 mph or higher, 11 of 102 mph or more and three at 103-plus mph.
Warming up in the bullpen, he couldn't take in the introductions before Milwaukee's first World Series game in 44 years. He thought about how far he had come, how he was at Double-A Biloxi two years ago.
“It was crazy," he said. “It’s everything I dreamed of.”
___

item.content:encoded:
If you expected the Milwaukee Brewers to enter the World Series without making any adjustments, you must not have been watching the team this season. Even after sweeping the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS and overcoming a red-hot Padres squad in the Division Series, manager Pat Murphy is always finding new ways to keep his opponents on their toes.
The Brewers released their batting order on Friday afternoon, just hours before first pitch. Their updated order will be as follows:
1. Jackson Chourio
2. Jake Bauers
3. Christian Yelich
4. William Contreras
5. Brice Turang
6. Garrett Mitchell
7. Cooper Pratt
8. Sal Frelick
9. David Hamilton
What should we take away from the Milwaukee Brewers' updated batting order for Game 1 of the World Series?
This new-look order should give the Brewers an interesting dynamic of staggering lefty and righty batters, likely in hopes of keeping Game 1 starter Nick Martinez, a righty, out of a consistent rhythm to begin the contest. By moving Contreras to fourth, it sets up Milwaukee's best home run hitter this postseason for a grand slam opportunity, should it arise. Meanwhile, Yelich at the third spot gives the Brew Crew a likely opportunity for some much-needed contact hitting early in the rotation.
It's far from surprising to see first baseman Jake Bauers taking such a firm position near the top of the batting order, as Bauers emerged as one of the most reliable offensive threats on the team, and frankly, in all of baseball. His ability to extend the pitch count and make contact persistently has been a thorn in the sides of pitchers everywhere, so this is likely Murphy's best attempt to extend Martinez's pitch count early.
Meanwhile, Turang slotting back into the fifth spot in the lineup makes sense given his inconsistent production thus far in the postseason. Through eight games, the 26-year-old is hitting just .222 with six hits to seven strikeouts. The good news, however, is that Turang turned a corner in the Dodgers series, logging hits in three of four hits, while scoring a run in each contest.
The end of the lineup should be of interest as well. All year long, Brewers fans grappled with questions over David Hamilton's place in the lineup, but through the postseason, he's certainly proving he belongs. Milwaukee is in serious need of some production late in the order, so all eyes will be on Hamilton, as well as Cooper Pratt and Sal Frelick, to carry that torch.
Overall, this is a wise move by Pat Murphy to make sure his lineup isn't identical to what Tampa Bay was expecting to see. Although the players are the same, a little shake-up in the order might force Martinez and the Rays' defense to think twice, which is all the Brewers can really ask for in a matchup of two teams that are this talented defensively.

As someone who married into a family of Rays fans and will be in Florida with my wife’s family for Halloween I would love to say the Rays will win in seven and I will watch that game with her family, but it is hard to vote against the Brewers. item.content:encoded:
Another season is coming to a close – the World Series is here. The Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays, both vying for their first championship. Who do we think will win? In how many games? Who will get MVP? Here are our thoughts.
As someone who married into a family of Rays fans and will be in Florida with my wife’s family for Halloween I would love to say the Rays will win in seven and I will watch that game with her family, but it is hard to vote against the Brewers.
They have the better offense. They have the better starting pitching. They have the deeper bullpen. They may even be better defensively. And they are going to be a bit more rested.
Because I will be on an airplane for game six I will say that the Brewers will win in six games.
The fun WSMVP choice would be Aaron Ashby continuing to dominate and taking the award by storm but a reliever has not won the WSMVP since Mariano Rivera in 1999 and Ashby is not the team’s primary closer.
So I will go with Jacob Misiorowski throwing two elite starts in games one and five, as well as an impact relief appearance in game six.
I think these teams are pretty evenly matched – the Rays have the upper hand in starting pitching, the Brewers have the better bullpen. While the Brewers scored more runs in the regular season, the teams had similar rate stats (Milwaukee had a 105 OPS+, compared to Tampa Bay’s 103). The Rays’ starters have consistently worked deeper into games compared to Milwaukee, and I wonder at what point the wear and tear will start to get to the Brewers’ bullpen. The Rays don’t strike out often, which leads me to believe they can be the team that finally conquers Milwaukee’s relievers. Milwaukee’s offense was relentless against the Dodgers, so it won’t be easy for the Rays to keep the Brewers down.
Overall, I think this will be a hard-fought series, with the Rays emerging victorious in seven games. Drew Rasmussen will win World Series MVP, winning his starts in Game 1 and Game 5, then coming out of the bullpen to pitch in Game 7.
Brewers in 7, Jackson Chourio is MVP. I wish Bob Uecker was here to see it.
Brewers in six. This should be a really fun and competitive series between two teams who play baseball the right way. Pitching wins, especially in the postseason, so Jacob Misiorowski will win the MVP after authoring his postseason legacy with two elite starts and a gutsy appearance out of the bullpen with everything on the line.
Brewers in 6. Christian Yelich wins MVP as he lives up to his newly minted captain status. Tampa will give them a run for their money!
Rays in 7. Freddy Peralta World Series MVP, because why not. He enters in desperation relief to get the final out.

item.title: [CBS Sports] The state of the outfield position heading into 2027: Pete Crow-Armstrong leads a talented but thin field

item.content:encoded:
There were 13 outfield-eligible players worth at least $20 in the FanGraphs Player Rater in 2026, just two fewer than the first base spot. If you remember that you only need to start one first baseman (and potentially a corner infielder and DH) while you might need to start as many as five outfielders at a time, well, you can see why this is problematic.
That's not to say the outfield is somehow a wasteland for Fantasy right now. First base was unusually strong in 2026, but in 2025, there were three times as many $20 players with outfield eligibility as at first base. And it's worth noting that the 13 $20 outfielders in 2026 are actually a few more than 2025's nine.
On the whole, I look at outfield as a position with a decent amount of depth in a three-outfielder, 12-team league. You should be able to draft a full lineup without feeling too bad about your outfield options in that formula.
Once you start getting into five-outfielder leagues, and especially deeper leagues with 15 teams, it starts to feel a lot more thin. That's to be expected, of course, but it's important to keep that in mind when you're preparing for the 2027 season. You don't have to make the position a priority in every draft, but if you aren't cognizant of it, you could end up with a real weakness in those deeper leagues.
For more on the state of the outfield position, .
2026 Outfield Review
- Pete Crow-Armstrong, CHC: .280 - 119 - 45 - 107 - 41
- Yordan Alvarez, HOU: .316 - 105 - 42 - 106 - 1
- Fernando Tatis Jr., SDP: .289 - 96 - 25 - 83 - 38
- Randy Arozarena, SEA: .281 - 113 - 26 - 79 - 26
- Jordan Walker, STL: .269 - 97 - 29 - 102 - 22
- James Wood, WSN: .265 - 106 - 30 - 77 - 21
- Jackson Chourio, MIL: .291 - 96 - 25 - 75 - 23
- Alec Burleson, STL: .279 - 89 - 26 - 116 - 4
- Jake McCarthy, COL: .291 - 80 - 15 - 83 - 32
- Michael Harris II, ATL: .294 - 79 - 26 - 87 - 12
- Jackson Merrill, SDP: .254 - 86 - 26 - 87 - 27
- Bryce Harper, PHI: .269 - 93 - 29 - 87 - 7
- Jake Bauers, MIL: .266 - 93 - 26 - 86 - 11
- Seiya Suzuki, CHC: .270 - 96 - 26 - 86 - 3
- Carson Benge, NYM: .282 - 86 - 20 - 65 - 22
- Andy Pages, LAD: .274 - 75 - 23 - 85 - 13
- Corbin Carroll, ARI: .239 - 91 - 22 - 78 - 21
- Oneil Cruz, PIT: .280 - 65 - 20 - 67 - 30
- Daylen Lile, WSN: .246 - 81 - 22 - 89 - 15
- Jac Caglianone, KCR: .289 - 72 - 23 - 75 - 7
- Bryan Reynolds, PIT: .261 - 102 - 17 - 72 - 9
- Chandler Simpson, TBR: .306 - 66 - 0 - 38 - 46
- Riley Greene, DET: .280 - 79 - 21 - 75 - 3
- Ceddanne Rafaela, BOS: .285 - 67 - 16 - 70 - 17
"Marginal player signs with the Rockies and has a Coors Field-inflated career season" used to be a pretty reliable archetype. Still, the Rockies have given Fantasy players little to get excited about in recent years. Jake McCarthy stands out as a notable exception, as his contact-and-speed profile proved to be a perfect fit for Coos Field. We're talking about relatively easy career-best production across the board, in a way that feels relatively obvious in retrospect. I don't have a ton of faith that this would prove replicable in any other ballpark — the gap between his .321 expected wOBA and his .349 actual mark was the 20th biggest in baseball — but it works there. As long as he isn't traded, McCarthy is a good bet to replicate his 2026 success.
I also want to highlight Harris and Merrill, because it feels very natural to group them together. They're both younger than you might realize – Harris will turn 26 shortly before his sixth MLB season in March, while Merrill won't even be 24 on Opening Day. They're also both linked by the combination of plus athleticism and bat speed, plus pretty poor approaches at the plate. They are, on the whole, capable of overcoming their poor swing decisions with outlier outcomes when they make contact, but that isn't always the case for either. Hence, the lengthy slumps that have held both back in recent years. They both got the good end of their range of outcomes in 2026, and we saw how high the ceiling can be for both. But drafting either for their 2026 outcome will carry inherent risks until they show some growth in their plate discipline.
Biggest Breakout from 2026
Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs
How could it be anyone else? Crow-Armstrong went from being a talented but deeply flawed hitter to arguably the best player in baseball, and he did it in-season. Early on, he looked more or less like the same guy he had always been, walking just nine times in 128 plate appearances through the end of June; he walked at least 12 times in each of the final five months of the season, something he had never done in any of his previous 13 months. He did that without sacrificing the pull-side power that has long been a key part of his game, and it turned him into one of the most dominant hitters in the game. Expecting all of those gains to carry over into 2027 might be asking a bit much — sometimes guys just get super locked in for a while — but he's clearly a much-improved hitter, and one who should be the first player taken in every single Roto league in 2027. And he shouldn't go much later in points leagues, where he was also the top player in 2026.
Honorable Mention: Jordan Walker, Cardinals
Okay, so if it were going to be anyone but Crow-Armstrong, it would be Walker, who went from being one of the biggest prospect busts in recent seasons to one of the best players in Fantasy. Walker still had pretty bad plate discipline and swing-and-miss issues, but he overcame that by being more aggressive early in the count and by doing more damage when he did make contact. The plate discipline issues and a late-season swoon — his expected wOBA dropped from .374 to .290 from the first half to the second — hint at the kind of risk involved in buying fully into what he did in 2026, and I suspect I'll be a little lower on him than the consensus. On the other hand, those were the exact reasons I cited to avoid Crow-Armstrong before the season, and look how that turned out. There's something to be said for just betting on the young, super-talented players when they show it.
Biggest Bust from 2026
The overall numbers don't show it, but Judge looked more or less like himself before he started dealing with that rib injury. In March and April, he posted a .450 xwOBA, right in line with his typical mark, but then things went downhill even before he ultimately went on the IL with a fractured rib. Was his downturn because of the injury? If so, then I think you can still make the case for him as a top-five pick in any league. But we're talking about a guy who will be 35 early next season, coming off a largely lost season that also came with an apparent decline in the underlying skill level, and that's a lot of red flags to overlook in a top-five pick. I might end up with Judge ranked that way come the spring, but it won't feel good.
Honorable Mention: Kyle Tucker, Dodgers
Maybe you don't think he was worth the contract the Dodgers gave him. Fair enough; you won't be alone in holding that opinion. But anyone who tells you there was any way to see this kind of disaster coming from Tucker is just lying to you. A 29-year-old went out and posted the worst batting average, on-base percentage, and slugging percentage of his career, and in two of those cases, it wasn't even close. Tucker had the combination of bat speed, athleticism, and plate discipline that should protect him against this kind of drop-off. Maybe the lights in L.A. were too bright for him. Maybe the pressure of the contract got to him. But I don't believe Tucker has just completely lost the ability to be an impact player, and he's still in what should be one of the best lineups in baseball, so I'll buy the bounce-back at what should be a steeply discounted price. The fact that he put together an excellent September and a very good postseason run certainly makes that an easier story to tell, of course.
Biggest rankings movers from 2026 to 2027
Up: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs; Yordan Alvarez, Astros; Jordan Walker, Cardinals; Jake Bauers, Brewers
As maybe the biggest Yordan Alvarez believer in the entire Fantasy industry coming into 2026, I do worry there's going to be a big overcorrection on him in 2027. We didn't learn anything new about Alvarez. If you think 2026 was a breakout season of some sort for him, I'm sorry, but you just weren't paying attention; he's just always been this good. His .442 xwOBA was higher than his career average, sure, but it was also not even the highest of his career, and he had a separate season with a .436 mark, too. The skills have always been there, but the difference is that he stayed healthy in 2026 after a bunch of injuries in previous seasons. I'm thrilled that he stayed healthy, and the fact that he did it in a season when his standing among Fantasy players was never lower is a good reminder that the Fantasy community isn't nearly as good at predicting who will and won't stay healthy as we think. But that will also be true in 2027: He'll be a top-five pick in most leagues despite the injury risk not being substantially different than it was last season. That's not to say he shouldn't be a top-five pick, of course; it's to say that he should have been a lot closer to a top-five pick last season than he was.
You could make a case for Bauers as the biggest breakout at outfield, because he was viewed as an even bigger afterthought than Walker was. He was a 30-year-old platoon specialist, after all! That he somehow went out in 2026 and put up a .901 OPS against lefties and had the best season of his career by a mile came completely out of nowhere, and it's going to be very interesting to see what the market for him as a free agent looks like this offseason. I buy a lot of what he did in 2026, and I suspect there will be enough skepticism around it to keep his price pretty reasonable. But betting on age-30 breakouts is historically a pretty bad idea, so you'll have to get a pretty big discount on what he did in 2026 to make him worth the risk, I think.
Down: Ronald Acuna, Braves; Kyle Tucker, Dodgers; Wyatt Langford, Rangers; Brent Rooker, Athletics
I wanted to make Langford one of the biggest bust picks, if only to highlight the fact that he has almost certainly been the least profitable pick in Fantasy over the past three years. He has struggled to stay healthy and just hasn't been the impact player you'd expect from a guy who had the kind of prospect pedigree he did — not to mention the benefit of the doubt the Fantasy community has continued to give him. I suspect that will come to an end in 2027, and … it kind of makes me more excited about buying into him this season. Because, for as frustrating and disappointing as he's been as a big-leaguer, his per-162 game pace for his career is pretty terrific: 90 runs, 24 homers, 24 steals, and 77 RBI. If he just does that in 2027, isn't that worth something like a fifth-round pick? And I don't think that's the ceiling for Langford, who has put up those numbers at a very young age while playing through a variety of injuries and has certainly flashed a higher ceiling at times. I'm not trying to excuse his poor performance; I'm just pointing out that all he has to do is stay healthy to be a very good Fantasy option. That's usually a good player to buy into at a discount.
The notoriously frugal A's are surely feeling some degree of buyer's remorse on Rooker's contract, but that contract should assure that he continues to play every day for them. His disappointing season came to an end after just 48 games, but he was on pace for another 30-homer season despite the injury. The .200 average is a tough look, as was the career-worst 32% strikeout rate, and the big drop off as a 31-year-old will rightly lead to plenty of skepticism around the potential of a bounce back. But that will also mean Rooker will come at a huge discount, potentially with a price outside the top 200 in many drafts. I'll buy that dip, personally. If you can buy him as a very cheap bench bat, there's no downside.
Offseason preview
Who needs an upgrade most?
A bunch of these teams are straddling the line between trying to go for it and needing to rebuild. The Reds could very well be in the market for a big upgrade in the outfield, or they could decide to move Elly De La Cruz and hit the reset button (again). The Astros could decide to give it one more run with this core, or they could move Alvarez and pivot to the future. The Phillies seem most likely to try to take a big swing, if only because Dave Dombrowski only knows how to take big swings. However, the Cardinals loom as a team that is ascending and could decide to get involved in the free-agent market with their core of cost-controlled position players.
Top impending free agents
- Randy Arozarena
- Seiya Suzuki
- Ian Happ
- Jake Bauers
- Trent Grisham
- Daulton Varsho
- Luis Robert
- Ramon Laureano
- George Springer
Arozarena is such a fascinating free agent. He's coming off a perfectly timed career-best season, but he'll be 32 before Opening Day and has rated out as a pretty terrible defender for several years running. There's probably no chance he gets anything more than a five-year contract in free agency, and he might need to agree to a move to DH as soon as 2027, two things that might be a tough pill to swallow. But having the best season of his career in the toughest offensive environment in baseball is no small thing, and nobody can deny his flair for the dramatic would be a great fit for a team with championship aspirations. The underlying skill set doesn't look so different from previous seasons, but his price will likely be higher than ever, making him one of the more obvious players to avoid in drafts for 2027, no matter where he lands.
Suzuki and, to a lesser extent, Happ look like players who will carry pretty solid value in Fantasy no matter where they land, but everyone else looks pretty context-dependent. Varsho's pull-heavy swing (and elite center field defense) would be a perfect fit for the Yankees, for example, but would be a much less interesting profile elsewhere. Stay tuned.
Trade candidates 
- Yordan Alvarez, Astros
- Jarren Duran, Red Sox
- Steven Kwan, Guardians
- Byron Buxton, Twins
- Brent Rooker, Athletics
- Jake McCarthy, Rockies
Alvarez feels like the biggest wild card here. The Astros won the AL West, but with just a .500 record, and they had such a poor showing in a two-game Wild Card round loss to the White Sox that the hometown crowd showered them with boos along the way. The Astros have lost their long-held edge over the competition, and while Alvarez's contract isn't expiring, he only has two years left on a relatively below-market deal. So this might be their last chance to maximize their return for him. The Astros are in flux in a lot of ways after firing Dana Brown, so they might not be positioned to make a big, franchise-altering move, but they would probably be best served trying to get off the treadmill of mediocrity sooner rather than later.
It increasingly looks like the Red Sox should have traded Duran at least a year ago, if not longer. All of a sudden, he's a 30-year-old corner outfielder who probably shouldn't play every day against lefties, and while he'll likely still earn a below-market salary in arbitration, he no longer looks like a real bargain. His skill set still has plenty of value for Fantasy (20 homers, 21 steals will always play), and I'd bet on him improving on last year's .207 average, but this isn't an early-round profile anymore.
Top rookies to know for 2026
- Josue De Paula, Dodgers
- Walker Jenkins, Twins
- Eduardo Quintero, Dodgers
- Theo Gillen, Rays
- Mike Sirota, Dodgers
- Zyhir Hope, Tigers
- Edward Florentino, Pirates
- Eric Hartman, Braves
- Drew Burress, Athletics
- Josiah Hartshorn, Cubs
- Lazaro Montes, Mariners
Jenkins is probably the most likely player here to be in an Opening Day lineup – I'm not sure what would have to happen for him not to be there, absent injury. He didn't take the league by storm in his first 26 games, but he was actually pretty great once he got adjusted, hitting .385/.400/.615 with just three strikeouts over his final 10 games. He has power, speed, and an excellent approach at the plate and should be a popular breakout candidate for 2027.
But not as popular as De Paula could be. I say "could" because, well, there's no obvious place for him to play. It's definitely not going to be in right field or DH, and slotting De Paula in at left field would require finding somewhere for Teoscar Hernandez and his large salary to go. Center field is the biggest hole in the Yankees outfield, but De Paula hasn't played there since 2023, and … well, you see the problem here. De Paula destroyed Double-A and very much passed the eye test in 11 MLB games, earning not-totally-unfair comparisons to Juan Soto and Yordan Alvarez for his approach at the plate. He could be an absolute star, but given the roster crunch and the fact that he's only 21 and hasn't played at Triple-A yet, this might be a situation like Junior Caminero's a few years back – remember, he debuted toward the end of the 2023 season but wasn't an everyday player until August of 2024. I hope it doesn't take that long, but we'll have to at least consider the possibility that it will.

item.content:encoded:
Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski ridiculously did something 89% of the time with 102+ MPH fastball originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays will meet in the World Series, starting Friday night in what's expected to be one of the more exciting World Series we've seen in quite some time.
Based on talent and other factors, both teams are equally matched, with small markets and young superstar talent.
For the Brewers, there might not be a bigger young superstar pitcher in Major League Baseball than Jacob Misiorowski. All Misiorowski has done this year is throw baseball at a ridiculous level, with the expectation that he'll win the National League Cy Young Award.
Misiorowski hasn't been bad by any means in the postseason, but also hasn't been great. He's thrown only 8.1 innings in his first two starts, with at least 88 pitches in each.
He still only allowed one earned run against the Los Angeles Dodgers and two against the San Diego Padres.
Misiorowski arguably has the best fastball in Major League Baseball, with some even thinking he has, or could have, the best in MLB history. As for what he's done this season, he's thrown more pitches at 102+ mph than nearly every other starter in baseball history, which is flat-out ridiculous.
"There have been 412 pitches thrown by MLB starters at 102+ MPH in the entire pitch tracking era and Jacob Misiorowski threw 365 of them this season. It's completely ridiculous," Codify Baseball wrote.
The biggest question Misiorowski will have to answer in the World Series is whether he can stay on the mound for six-plus innings.
Even during parts of the regular season, it wasn't exactly like this was a workhorse throwing complete games left and right. He hasn't thrown more than 6.1 innings in any start since Aug. 2, though multiple factors could explain it, as the Brewers arguably have the best bullpen in Major League Baseball and trust a lot of guys coming in during the back half of games.

item.title: [mlb.com] Our experts make their World Series predictions
item.dc:creator: Max Ralph

item.content:encoded:
The Brewers, whose 103 regular-season wins were a franchise record, navigated a tight NL Division Series against the Padres before clobbering the two-time reigning champion Dodgers in the NL Championship Series sweep. It’s just the second World Series appearance in their history and their first since 1982.
Meanwhile, the Rays swept the division rival Yankees in the ALDS before handling the Guardians in six games in the ALCS. They’re back in the Fall Classic for the third time and the first since 2020.
Both teams do a little bit of everything right on the diamond, making for what should be a thoroughly exciting World Series. Here’s how our group of MLB.com experts see it playing out.
Rays vs. Brewers
The pick: Brewers (43 of 51 votes, 84.3%)
Why they’ll win
Any time you take down the back-to-back reigning champs, and do so in a sweep, it’s going to make noise. But really, this is nothing new for the 2026 Brewers. They owned the best regular-season record with a roster that just gets the job done across the board.
The Brewers can play small ball, but they can slug when it matters most, too. In fact, Milwaukee has been more homer-dependent in October than it was all year. But the club can still work a deep count and get on base in many ways. Just ask Jake Bauers.
On the mound, it’s no secret that the bullpen is the Brewers’ strength. One of the best groups in the regular season is only doing more of the same in October, with a 1.33 ERA in eight games. Lefty Aaron Ashby is leading the charge during a historically good run. And then there’s that Jacob Misiorowski guy, who has been good enough in the playoffs but could unleash a new, dominant level in the World Series.
What they’re saying
“There's something about this Brewers club. Maintaining the league's best record all summer and barely giving an inch so far in the postseason, they're looking pretty unstoppable with the right mix of clutch hits, key performers and an absolutely lockdown bullpen. It might finally be the Crew's moment in the spotlight.” -- Adrian Garro, editorial producer
“The Brewers have been knocking on this door for years and are firing on all cylinders following their impressive sweep of the Dodgers. They are smart and hard-nosed enough not to let the long layoff affect them negatively.” -- Andrew Werle, supervising editor, content operations
“Walking off Mason Miller. Sweeping the 2-time defending champion Dodgers. These Brewers may just be a team of destiny, with their final obstacle being the American League's top-seeded Rays.” -- Kyle Boris, supervisor, media operations
The dissenting view
The Brewers have been dominant, but so have the Rays. They have a clear edge in starting pitching, with Drew Rasmussen, Freddy Peralta and Nick Martinez firing on all cylinders. The Tampa Bay bullpen, while not as overpowering as the Brewers’, is still strong and has lockdown closer Bryan Baker waiting in the wings.
The key for the Rays likely lies in their lineup, where Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda appear to be heating up at the right time. Much like Milwaukee, the Rays will put together quality at-bats, get on base and then cause havoc on the basepaths. Perhaps no one is more adept at doing so than Chandler Simpson.
“The Rays' ‘small ball’ doesn't slump, and they've been pressing all of the right pitching buttons.” -- Jonathan Mayo, national reporter, prospects
“With their Big 3 of Yandy Díaz, Jonathan Aranda and Junior Caminero breaking out at the end of the ALCS -- plus a slight edge over the Crew in starting pitching -- I believe the Rays are going to steal Game 1 vs. The Miz and ride that to a World Series title. Third time is a charm.” -- Brian McGrath, supervising editor, content operations
Series predictions
Brewers (6 games): 23 votes
Brewers (7 games): 14 votes
Brewers (5 games): 5 votes
Rays (7 games): 4 votes
Rays (6 games): 3 votes
Rays (5 games): 1 vote
Brewers (4 games): 1 vote
There may have been an overwhelming majority of our group predicting the Brewers to win the World Series, but that doesn’t do justice to how close these two teams seem to be. This will: 44 of 51 voters see the series going at least six games.
Who will be named World Series MVP?
Jackson Chourio (MIL): 16 votes
William Contreras (MIL): 13 votes
Jacob Misiorowski (MIL): 6 votes
Yandy Díaz (TB): 5 votes
Brice Turang (MIL): 5 votes
Aaron Ashby (MIL): 1 vote
Jake Bauers (MIL): 1 vote
Junior Caminero (TB): 1 vote
Trevor Megill (MIL): 1 vote
Drew Rasmussen (TB): 1 vote
Chandler Simpson (TB): 1 vote
It’s not hard to see why Chourio was our experts’ favorite to take home the World Series Most Valuable Player Award. Still just 22 years old, Chourio already leads Brewers franchise history with six career playoff home runs. He’s already shown he can rise to the occasion this year with a walk-off single against Mason Miller in the NLDS and a massive homer against Blake Snell in the NLCS. But Chourio’s overall production this October has been quiet (6-for-35). It might just be a matter of time before he breaks out.
“Chourio is due to break out in the World Series. While he hasn't done much in the playoffs so far, his two homers were impactful -- a go-ahead shot and a game-tying blast. He's ready to let it rip.” -- Kelsie Heneghan, senior coordinator, social media editorial, MiLB
“He's a legend in the making. This is the start of his Hall of Fame case.” -- Will Leitch, senior columnist
Who will be on the mound when the series ends … and what happens?
Trevor Megill (MIL), final out: 24 votes
Aaron Ashby (MIL), final out: 10 votes
Bryan Baker (TB), final out: 6 votes
Jacob Misiorowski (MIL), final out: 6 votes
Bryan Baker (TB), walked off: 3 votes
Drew Rasmussen (TB), final out: 1 vote
Ian Seymour (TB), final out: 1 vote
Megill has been lights-out as the Brewers’ closer, so it’s easy to envision him shutting things down at American Family Field in Game 6 or 7. But don’t be surprised if it’s Ashby continuing his fireman role -- or The Miz coming in for a clutch relief appearance.

item.title: [Orlando Sentinel] Christian Yelich’s simple World Series message for title-less Brewers: Expect to be here
item.dc:creator: Associated Press
item.description: By STEVE MEGARGEE MILWAUKEE (AP) — Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy was celebrating his team’s World Series appearance when he shared that recently crowned team captain Christian Yelich had predicted this moment several months before. “Yeli said it early in the season,” Murphy said after the Brewers completed their NL Championship Series sweep of the Dodgers. “He said, ‘You’d better start believing because we’re going to the World Series,’ and we’re right here.” There’s only one problem with
item.content:encoded:
By STEVE MEGARGEE
MILWAUKEE (AP) — Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy was celebrating his team’s World Series appearance when he shared that recently crowned team captain Christian Yelich had predicted this moment several months before.
“Yeli said it early in the season,” Murphy said after the Brewers completed their NL Championship Series sweep of the Dodgers. “He said, ‘You’d better start believing because we’re going to the World Series,’ and we’re right here.”
There’s only one problem with this narrative. Yelich can’t recall making that proclamation.
“I don’t remember,” Yelich said Thursday, the day before the Brewers host the Tampa Bay Rays in their first World Series game since 1982. “He told me I said that. I don’t know. But I think throughout the year, you just believed that. I think you have to believe that and you have to expect to be here. You don’t want to approach it like, ‘Wow, I can’t believe we’re here.’ You should expect to be here, especially with the kind of team we’ve had.”
Whether Yelich actually said it or not, the fact his perceived comment would carry such weight comes as no surprise.
Yelich, 34, and pitcher Brandon Woodruff are the only players who have been on Milwaukee’s roster throughout the Brewers’ run of eight playoff appearances in nine seasons. The Brewers acquired him from Miami in 2018, and he was named NL MVP later that year. Yelich’s value in the clubhouse has remained as strong as ever, even as he’s battled injuries over the last several years and a drop in production this season.
Getting selected as Brewers’ first captain
Teammates say the Brewers’ decision to name Yelich the first team captain in franchise history on the final weekend of the regular season merely formalized what they already knew.
“He’s been a captain before he got the ‘C,’” outfielder Sal Frelick said. “We all know that.”
He’s one of three active captains in MLB, joining the New York Yankees’ Aaron Judge and the Kansas City Royals’ Salvador Perez.
Yelich’s appreciation for Brewers history was evident from the way he reacted to this honor. When the idea was proposed to Yelich, he initially wanted to make sure it was OK with Hall of Fame shortstop Robin Yount, who never had the captain title but is regarded as the best Brewers player ever.
Yount called Yelich’s concern “a very humbling” gesture that “certainly wasn’t necessary.”
“He certainly deserved that, earned that on his own,” Yount said. “The fact that the Brewers chose to actually give a captain’s ‘C’ on his jersey, and all of that. I think it’s great. I think the timing couldn’t have been better for something like this.”
Now Yelich is playing a major role in helping the Brewers get back to the World Series for the first time since Yount led them there during his MVP season of 1982. This hasn’t been a banner season for Yelich, whose .315 on-base percentage and .692 OPS were career lows.
Stepping up in postseason
But he has been coming through lately.
Yelich ended a string of 18 straight postseason games without an RBI when he singled home a run in Game 3 of the NL Division Series at San Diego. He has gone 7 for 24 at the plate this postseason, a .292 average that eclipses his regular-season average of .235.
Murphy says he noticed how much the “C” meant to Yelich.
“It was real for him,” Murphy said. “You can tell when you give someone something or you let somebody know something. It was real for Yelich, in a way that I was even shocked at. Since then, I don’t know the numbers, but I just know this guy is on point. He’s focused.
“He feels that responsibility. And I think it’s an easier responsibility for him to carry, because it’s so natural, than to try to carry the pressure of, ‘Hey, I’ve got to get four hits or I’ve got to do this.’ He’s way more important to this process than anyone knows.”
Yelich has been setting an example to his younger teammates for years.
“He took me under his wing my first big-league camp before I was even in the big leagues,” Frelick said. “Walking me through baserunning stuff. I’m like, ‘This guy has won an MVP. Why is he telling me how tight I have to cut the third-base bag when I’m running home from second?’ It’s because he just knows how to play the game. He cares. He knows that’s how to win baseball games. And he knows that if people hear it coming from him, they’ll then tell other guys how important it is.”
That kind of approach had Yelich and his younger teammates believing they could reach a World Series. Now they’re finally here.
“This is the expectation and the standard we wanted to set going into spring training,” Yelich said. “It isn’t like we woke up and found ourselves here. This was the goal and where we wanted to be.”
___

item.title: [prpeak.com] World Series preview: Surprising Brewers-Rays matchup will open with Jacob Misiorowski's record heat
item.dc:creator: Ronald Blum; The Associated Press
item.description: MILWAUKEE (AP) — The Miz will try to whiz his famous fastball by batters on baseball's biggest stage, opening a new-look World Series between teams guaranteed to produce a first-time champion. Jacob Misiorowski brings his record-setting heat to the mound for the Milwaukee Brewers on Friday night when he throws the first pitch of the best-of-seven championship against the Tampa Bay Rays, a matchup of modest-money marvels who bumped off glamorous rivals with a throwback base-to-base style. “Forres
item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE (AP) — The Miz will try to whiz his famous fastball by batters on baseball's biggest stage, opening a new-look World Series between teams guaranteed to produce a first-time champion.
Jacob Misiorowski brings his record-setting heat to the mound for the Milwaukee Brewers on Friday night when he throws the first pitch of the best-of-seven championship against the Tampa Bay Rays, a matchup of modest-money marvels who bumped off glamorous rivals with a throwback base-to-base style.
“Forrest Gump, everyone,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said Thursday, introducing his ace to the assembled media.
“I'm still fresh to all of this and I have no idea what the hell is going on,” Misiorowski said a few minutes later.
Few predicted this pairing of pennant winners when the season opened March 25. The first World Series with robot umpires is the first since 1980 between teams seeking their first championship and also could be the first with a 104 mph pitch — thanks to Misiorowski — and the first to be played totally indoors.
Milwaukee is in the Series for the second time after a 44-year absence — an appropriate number given that it was the jersey of the Cream City's most famous baseball player, Hank Aaron, who became a star with the Milwaukee Braves in the 1950s and ended his career with the expansion Brewers in the 1970s.
Both teams fell short in previous Series trips, the Brewers losing to St. Louis in 1982 and the Rays to Philadelphia in 2008 and to the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2020. Not since the Phillies beat Kansas City in 1980 have two teams met seeking their first title. The time before that was in 1920.
Rays players are excited to display their brand of baseball.
“We love watching those guys cause chaos,” Tampa Bay pitcher Steven Matz said of his team's bunters and speedsters. “Every time it’s first and third and someone lays down a bunt, we are just dying laughing in the bullpen.”
Misiorowski is likely to set a World Series velocity record
Misiorowski, a 24-year-old right-hander in his first full major league season, is a starting pitcher like no other. He threw 1,115 pitches of 100 mph or higher this year — shattering the old high of 673 since tracking began in 2008, by Jordan Hicks in 2018.
His fastest pitch was 105.5 mph to the Chicago Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 27, and he appears likely to break the 101.1 mph record for a Series starter by the New York Mets' Noah Syndergaard in 2015 and possibly the overall Series high of 103.2 mph by Cubs reliever Aroldis Chapman to Cleveland's Coco Crisp in Game 2 of 2016.
Misiorowski didn't finish the fifth inning in either of his first two postseason starts this year. Batters have swung at 94 of his 182 postseason pitches and fouled off 51 — 28% of pitches and 54% of swings.
“He hasn’t been as crisp,” Murphy said. “They’re obviously looking at an area. They’re trying to exploit everything. He’s exposed, like all these guys get at some point.”
Martinez a surprise starter for Rays
Nick Martinez will start for Tampa Bay, which gives extra rest to Drew Rasmussen ahead of Game 2 and Freddy Peralta before Game 3.
A 36-year-old right-hander with his fourth major league team, Martinez took the Rays to dinner Wednesday at Carnevor, a top Milwaukee steakhouse. He invites teammates, who have nicknamed him “El Presidente,” to a restaurant in every road city.
“To when I first got to the league, I’ve been around guys that knew how to control a clubhouse and for lack of a better term, knew how to throw a party,” Martinez said. “Getting the guys together is important. Creating that off-the-field chemistry translates to on the field.”
Brewers and Rays have throwback offenses
In an age where power bats usually rule, Milwaukee scored a major league-low 32.1% of its runs on homers and Tampa Bay was second-lowest at 34.4%, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.
Brewers captain Christian Yelich says “we’ve done a good job of being kind of chameleons.”
“It's cool that you don't have to be the team to hit 170 home runs a game or whatever,” Misiorowski said. “You can win a baseball game so many different ways.”
Rays batters had the fewest strikeouts among the 30 teams and Tampa Bay’s 45 sacrifice bunts were the most among American League teams since 2015.
“If we had a club that was built with a bunch of boppers, we probably wouldn’t be bunting and stealing bases,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “I think we already have made bunting cool.”
After back-to-back Dodgers titles, MLB will have a small-payroll champion
This marks the first time since 1991 that both Series teams are in the bottom half of payrolls: the Brewers were 19th as of Aug. 31 and the Rays 25th. Milwaukee, MLB's smallest market, could become the first small-market champion since Kansas City in 2015. The Rays rank 15th in market size.
To reach the Series, the Brewers swept the deep-pocketed, two-time champion Dodgers in the NL Championship Series and the Rays swept the New York Yankees in an AL Division Series.
Yelich, the highest-paid player in the Series, was 44th overall in the majors on opening day. Yandy Díaz, who earns most among the Rays, ranked 154th.
Robot umps are changing games
Batters have succeeded on 63% of challenges during the postseason in the first year of the Automated Ball-Strike System, winning 40 of 63 appeals to the robot umps. That is up from 49% during the regular season.
Catchers' 58% success rate in the playoffs (58 of 99) is down a tick from 59% during the regular season and pitchers are 1 for 1 — Tampa Bay’s Griffin Jax made the only challenge. The 60% overall rate is up from 54% in the regular season.
Tampa Bay's batters have yet to make a postseason challenge. Milwaukee's have won 4 of 7, including a perfect 2 for 2 by Jake Bauers.
Brewers catcher William Contreras has won 60% (12 of 20) and Rays catcher Liam Hicks 67% (8 of 12).
Rest vs. rust: Extra time off hasn't been helpful in recent years
Milwaukee will have had seven days off going into the opener.
While teams with less rest are 15-15 in the Series since Wild Card Era started in 1995, they are 12-4 since 2009.
___
Ronald Blum, The Associated Press

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

23 Oct 2026, 04:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Benny Sieu)
MILWAUKEE -- The Milwaukee Brewers will be looking for hard-throwing Jacob Misiorowski to regain his dominant regular-season form against the visiting Tampa Bay Rays on Friday in the opening game of the World Series.
Misiorowski, who often tops 100 mph with his fastball, will be opposed by veteran right-hander Nick Martinez in a matchup of teams that have not won the World Series. It is the first meeting of two teams without a World Series title since the Philadelphia Phillies topped the Kansas City Royals in six games in 1980.
Milwaukee, which won a franchise-record 103 games during the regular season, advanced with a four-game sweep of the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series, while the Rays ousted the Cleveland Guardians in six games in the American League Championship Series.
The Brewers' only other World Series appearance was in 1982 when they were in the American League. The charismatic 'Harvey's Wallbangers' lost 6-3 to the St. Louis Cardinals in the decisive seventh game.
The Rays will be making their third World Series appearance. They lost to Philadelphia in five games in 2008 and in six games to the Dodgers in 2020.
Misiorowski, considered the favorite for the NL Cy Young Award, was 16-5 with a 1.80 ERA and 252 strikeouts. The latter two stats were best in the majors.
But the 24-year-old right-hander did not make it through five innings in either postseason start, although the Brewers rallied to win both games. They topped the San Diego Padres 3-2 in Game 1 of the National League Division Series and the Dodgers 2-1 in the NLCS opener.
'I feel good. I feel like the first one might have been a little under what I expected, but the second one was pretty much right where I wanted to be,' Misiorowski said.
Misiorowski worked out of trouble in his postseason starts, allowing three runs on nine hits in 8 1/3 innings with 11 strikeouts and four walks.
'He hasn't been as crisp,' Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said. 'I don't think people are up there thinking it's going to be 104 (mph), and I think they're elated if it's anything less than that. They're obviously looking at an area. They're trying to exploit everything. He's exposed, like all these guys get at some point.'
At the back end, the Brewers' bullpen has allowed six runs over 40 2/3 innings for a 1.33 ERA in the postseason. Closer Trevor Megill has four saves after collecting 30 in the regular season.
Milwaukee was last in the NL in home runs (154) during the regular season but leads all teams in the postseason with 10 homers in eight games. The Rays have hit seven in nine games.
Catcher William Contreras batted .367 with three homers and five RBIs over the Brewers' first two series. Outfielder Jackson Chourio hit .171, but he had two homers and a team-high seven RBIs.
Jake Bauers, who reached the majors with the Rays in 2018, was named the NLCS Most Valuable Player after hitting .286 with one homer and six RBIs against the Dodgers. Bauers set career highs with 26 homers and 86 RBIs during the regular season.
The 36-year-old Martinez pitched in the postseason with San Diego in 2022 and the Cincinnati Reds last season, but he will be making his World Series debut Friday. Ace Drew Rasmussen will start Game 2 with an extra day's rest, with former Brewers ace Freddy Peralta to follow in Game 3.
'It's exciting,' Martinez said Thursday. 'I think as a team, as a staff, we're confident in whoever we call up for the mound. It fell on me, and my job is just to rack up as many outs as we can and keep us in this ballgame.'
Martinez picked up the win in Game 4 of the ALCS when the Rays evened the series with a 7-3 victory at Cleveland. He allowed one run on two hits in 5 1/3 innings.
'He was pitching in pretty cold weather in Cleveland,' said Rays manager Kevin Cash, who was also at the helm for the 2020 World Series. 'Made some adjustments, he got the strike throwing where he wanted, the cutter gone, and the changeup. I don't even know, somebody told me he changed his grip in between innings, between the first and second. I'm glad I didn't know that in the moment.'
Martinez also started Game 3 in the Rays' ALDS sweep of the New York Yankees. He gave up two runs in 3 2/3 innings in an eventual 4-3 Tampa Bay victory.
Martinez is 0-1 with a 4.44 ERA in 12 regular-season games (seven starts) against Milwaukee. He has a 2.93 ERA in eight games at American Family Field.
Rays closer Bryan Baker, who tied for the MLB lead with 41 saves, has five saves in five postseason chances, pitching in seven of the nine games.
Third baseman Junior Caminero, whose 42 homers were second in the AL, has just one hit in 33 at-bats in the postseason.
--Jim Hoehn, Field Level Media
